newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan airport cargo handlers in go-slow protest.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan airport cargo handlers in go-slow protest.

text.p: Cargo handlers at Taiwan's main airport on Monday began refusing to work overtime or off-hours, saying that authorities had ignored their interests in privatising a state-run cargo centre.

The protest will hamper the handling of some 2,080 tonnes of exported and imported goods a day during a crush period before the Lunar New Year and could hurt some affect some 10,000 export firms, airport officials said.

"We apologise for the inconvenience we have caused, but the transport and the aviation authorities are to blame for failing to safeguard our interests," Chen Chin-lung, standing director of the cargo centre trade union, told Reuters.
The government plans on July 30 to privatise Taiwan's principal international cargo centre at the big international airport just south of the capital, Taipei.
Workers claim they will lose benefits accorded to government employees after centre businesses are turned over to the private sector.
"Until the transport ministry agrees to give proper compensation, we will continue to refuse overtime work, meaning we now only work between 8:30 a.m. and 6:00 p.m.," Chen said.
The centre normally operates 24 hours a day.
He said the ministry originally agreed to give them an answer on legitimate compensation at the end of January, but "they keep stalling, saying they need another month".
"Before they give us an answer, our protest will continue indefinitely," Chen noted.
A cargo centre official acknowledged that cargo handling would be slowed down, and at least one-third of all cargo loads would be affected.

"Our centre handles about 500,000 tonnes of cargo every year and the week before the Chinese New Year is extremely busy since a number of exporters want to ship their products abroad," the official said.
The centre normally handles 2,080 tonnes of cargo a day during the annual push before the Lunar New Year, which this year begins on February 7.
Vice-minister of transport Hsu Chieh-kuei urged calm, saying officials were doing all they could to help.
"The transport ministry is helping them to strive for their rights and interests, and the employees should be patient," he was quoted by state-funded television as saying.

Kao Li-jen, secretary-general of the Taiwan Export-Import Association, said what centre employees did was unfair to Taiwan industry since it would greatly affect the operations of some 10,000 export firms.
